items.context: The current 500ms calibration computes a simple average of all RMS samples. A single wind gust or car horn during this window permanently biases thresholds. We need a more robust estimator.

options.label: Median-based calibration with outlier rejection
options.rationale: Replace the arithmetic mean with the median of calibration samples, and discard samples > 2x the median before computing thresholds. Simple, effective for transient outliers, preserves the 500ms window. Recommended because it's minimal code change with maximum impact on the most common failure case (single loud noise during calibration).

options.label: Extended calibration with sliding window bootstrap
options.rationale: Extend calibration to 1-2 seconds and use the same sliding window + 25th percentile logic already in computeSlidingNoiseFloor. More samples = more robust, but delays speech detection start. Adds latency users will notice.

options.label: Re-calibration on threshold violation
options.rationale: Keep 500ms initial calibration but trigger automatic re-calibration if the first 2-3 seconds of post-calibration data show the thresholds are clearly wrong (e.g., no frames even close to speechThreshold). More complex state management but self-healing.

items.context: The fixed 1.5x (silence) and 3x (speech) multipliers on the noise floor work well in quiet environments but fail outdoors where speech-to-noise ratio is lower. The multipliers need to adapt to the ambient noise level.

options.label: Noise-level-dependent multipliers with a lookup curve
options.rationale: Define a simple piecewise function: at low noise floors (<0.02 RMS), use wide multipliers (1.5x/3x); at high noise floors (>0.05 RMS), compress to narrower multipliers (1.2x/2x). Interpolate between. Directly addresses the SNR problem in noisy environments. Recommended because it's tunable, testable, and handles the core failure mode.

options.label: Fixed but tuned multipliers
options.rationale: Lower the fixed multipliers (e.g., 1.3x/2.5x) to work better outdoors. Simplest change but may regress indoor accuracy by being too sensitive to quiet environmental sounds.

options.label: Spectral-based threshold (use frequency distribution, not just RMS)
options.rationale: Analyze the frequency content to distinguish speech from noise. Wind is low-frequency dominant; speech has formant peaks. More accurate but significantly more complex, requires FFT data the current VAD doesn't receive.

items.context: Currently, returning from watchingSilence to speechDetected requires RMS > speechThreshold (3x noise floor). This means a brief speech dip below the high threshold during a noisy moment causes the VAD to stay in watchingSilence and eventually time out, even though the user is still talking. A lower re-entry threshold would help.

options.label: Use silenceThreshold (1.5x) for re-entry from watchingSilence
options.rationale: If we're already watching silence and RMS rises above silenceThreshold, that's enough evidence speech resumed — we don't need the full speechThreshold proof. Simple one-line change. Recommended because it directly addresses the 'brief dip' failure mode with zero additional state.

options.label: Add a separate reEntryThreshold (e.g., 2x noise floor)
options.rationale: Midpoint between silence and speech thresholds. More conservative than A, gives a tunable knob, but adds another threshold to VadRefs.

options.label: Keep current behavior (no hysteresis)
options.rationale: If the adaptive multipliers (D2) sufficiently compress thresholds in noisy environments, the gap between silence and speech thresholds may be small enough that hysteresis is unnecessary.

items.text: The existing regression test ('does not inflate speechThreshold during sustained speech') already validates that the sliding window excludes speech-state samples. This is a solid foundation — our changes must not break this invariant.

The bandpass filter (80Hz-8kHz) in audioUtils.ts uses simple Butterworth biquad filters. Wind noise is predominantly <200Hz, so the 80Hz highpass already provides partial wind rejection. A more aggressive highpass (e.g., 150-200Hz) could improve outdoor performance but would attenuate male fundamental frequencies (~85-180Hz). This tradeoff is worth considering but is secondary to the threshold improvements.

plan_updates: Created initial plan scaffold with problem statement, root cause analysis, scope definition, risk matrix, and test plan outline. Approach section left TBD pending decisions on calibration strategy (D1), threshold model (D2), and re-entry hysteresis (D3).
